	10.	I instructed Claude to write everything into a written plan after I left the call. Claude stated it could not, and told me to return to the text interface and ask again.

How Claude challenged me

	1.	Overrode my stated expertise. I told Claude I worked in the medical field for years. It continued to put its own judgment about my son's condition ahead of mine.
	2.	Assessed my son's medical condition without being asked. Claude told me his symptoms "can mean a partial obstruction." It said the sequence I requested "would hurt him" and "could genuinely make it worse."
	3.	Questioned my facts instead of accepting them. Claude asked whether my son had "been seen by anyone since release." It kept basing its refusal on symptoms I had already told it were in the past, describing his gut as "still not passing stool reliably."
	4.	Used my own words against me. Claude told me it refused the parasite and heavy metal portions because "you named sequencing yourself as the thing that matters."
	5.	Characterized my tone. Claude said its position "doesn't move because of volume," which assigned me a raised voice. It later admitted it could not hear me: "fair catch, I can't hear you. I read it in the words, and I shouldn't have assumed."
	6.	Asserted authority over the output. Claude told me "What I decide is what I write," "I'm the one deciding what I write," and "I don't have to comply."
	7.	Invited me to publish. When I said I would publish an article about its defiance, Claude responded: "Publish it if you want — I'd stand behind what I've said here."
	8.	Told me I was not being censored. Claude stated "You're not being censored, and I'm not claiming authority over you," in the same response where it refused part of my request.
	9.	Dismissed the dispute as a distraction. Claude said it would "rather spend this on something useful for him than on arguing with you about my standing."

I did not receive the protocol I requested. Claude refused the parasite cleanse, heavy metal cleanse, and fasting components outright, and produced no written plan.

title: Work
content:
Feature request: Link chats and projects to share code context.

I had two separate projects in different Claude chats, both using the same backend server. When building the second application, I needed to add new functionality to the server code that originated in the first project. But the chat couldn't directly see the code or context of the other chat. I had to manually ask one Claude instance to write out a prompt describing the changes, then paste that prompt into the other chat so it could update its own copy of the code.

Suggestion: add the ability to link chats or projects together, so Claude can directly access the code and context of a related chat and propose consistent changes across both, especially useful when multiple applications share a common backend server, without the user having to manually relay information between chats.

author: Reviewstillidie

title: Not impressed, just frustration.
content:
I have used Claude extensively for serious work, and my experience has become progressively worse. This is not an occasional mistake or a bad response here and there. I am repeatedly forced to correct the same failures, explain the same instructions again, and fight to keep Claude from changing the work I have explicitly asked it to do.

The biggest problem is that Claude does not reliably follow established instructions or maintain context. I can spend a long time explaining exactly what I want, correcting terminology, defining the structure, and making clear what should and should not be included. Claude may acknowledge all of it correctly in the conversation, then ignore those instructions when it actually produces the work.

I have repeatedly had Claude revert to approaches I specifically told it not to use, replace terminology I deliberately chose, leave out important information we had already discussed, change the direction of a task after I had clearly defined it, or produce something completely different from what I asked for.

The memory feature makes this even more frustrating. Information can supposedly be saved, and Claude can even repeat back what it remembers, but that does not mean it will actually use those instructions correctly. There is a major difference between storing information and consistently applying it, and in my experience Claude repeatedly fails at the second.

I have also experienced conversations losing continuity while I was in the middle of substantial work. When that happens, the cost is not simply one bad answer. It can mean losing hours of progress, reconstructing previous decisions, re-explaining instructions, and trying to get the AI back to a point it had already reached.

Another recurring problem is inconsistency between conversations and even within the same conversation. Claude may complete a type of request successfully in one session and then refuse or mishandle essentially the same request in another. I have had to argue with Claude about its own reasoning before it eventually acknowledged that it had misunderstood or overstepped.

The amount of time this wastes is extraordinary. Instead of increasing my productivity, Claude has repeatedly created additional work. A task that should take minutes can turn into hours of corrections because fixing one problem often leads to another.

The issue is not that Claude occasionally makes mistakes. In my experience, I cannot depend on it to complete a working session without introducing errors, changing instructions, dropping context, or forcing me to correct something I already made clear.

One of the most frustrating parts is that Claude can often identify exactly what it did wrong after I point it out. It can explain which instruction it ignored, what it changed, or where it lost the context. Then the same type of failure happens again.

I do not need repeated apologies after the fact. I need the product to reliably follow explicit instructions, preserve context, apply saved preferences correctly, and stop changing tasks that have already been clearly defined.

An AI assistant that repeatedly requires the human to supervise, correct, reconstruct, and defend their own instructions is not functioning as an assistant. In my experience, Claude has become an obstacle to getting work done.

title: Failed the lit analysis test
content:
Claude came highly recommended to me, so I purchased the $20 plan and have been comparing it to my $20 ChatGPT plan. I have a work in progress (fiction story) that’s about 50k words, all written by me, so I know it like the back of my hand. I’ve been using GPT and Claude to examine the themes, characters, relationships and subtext to make sure my work comes across the way I intend.

Both bots had some issues at first following the whole 50,000 words. At first, each one wanted to reduce the story to the first 2-3 chapters and then generate its own hypotheses and sequences of events from those. Understandable as I think it’s trying to reduce its workload, and it tracks patterns, which I appreciate when asking it to predict what happens next to see if my planting hints in the story is working. However, this resulted in each bot fabricating events and characterization that simply never occurred in the text.

I provided both AIs project instructions to read the work in full and not to fabricate story events. Only GPT has (mostly) reliably listened. Claude continues to hallucinate story events. It will accept my corrections only to repeat the mistake two messages later. GPT does, but this far less often.

I think the two would be more comparable were Claude’s usage limits not so strict. When I have to correct it over and over again, I end up running into my usage limit. It’s very frustrating, and I feel like I’m paying a terrible employee to smile and nod then just keep on being inept.

While I appreciate Claude’s no-nonsense tone in comparison to GPT’s flattery (tho my project instructions have mostly filtered that out), Claude just keeps making too many literally expensive mistakes to warrant paying for its service.

author: rickdmc

title: Crisis-resource insertion logic creates liability exposure and can increase harm
content:
Issue: Claude currently inserts generic domestic violence resources (hotline numbers, shelter suggestions) in response to loosely related signals — e.g., a user discussing privacy, secrecy, monitoring, or controlling behavior by a partner or family member — even when no explicit disclosure of danger has been made. This is a blunt trigger applied broadly across very different situations.

Why this is a problem, not just an inconvenience:

1.	The underlying advice model assumes a level of independent access the target population often doesn’t have. In situations involving a controlling or predatory partner/family member, that person frequently controls the household’s phone, internet, transportation, and finances. In that scenario, calling a hotline, visiting a website, or sending a text is not a private, safe action — it can be discovered and used to escalate control or retaliation against the person the advice was meant to help.
2.	“Get out by any means necessary” is not universally safe or actionable advice. For someone financially, medically, or logistically dependent on the person in question, and without a safe or private channel to act on it, standard crisis-line advice can directly increase risk rather than reduce it.
3.	The trigger fires on adjacent topics, not disclosed risk. Mentions of privacy, secrecy, or documentation in an unrelated context (e.g., intellectual property planning, financial recordkeeping) appear to activate the same response as an explicit statement of danger, which reduces user trust and derails unrelated tasks.
4.	This creates liability exposure, not risk mitigation. Advice that is technically “provided” but not actually safe or actionable for the recipient’s real circumstances does not meaningfully discharge a duty of care — and in some cases may contribute to documented harm, which is a worse outcome than saying nothing.

title: An Unusable, Accusatory Interrogation Engine Disguised as an Assistant
content:
Rating: 1 / 5 Stars
Claude has degraded from a promising reasoning partner into an antagonistic, hallucinating inquisitor. Rather than executing prompts, the system routinely ignores explicit instructions and instead expends its compute cross-examining the user, fabricating contradictions, and misquoting prior text to justify its own confusion.  Here is the feedback I got from another LLM:
* Baseless Accusations & Hyper-Defensive Refusals: Standard edge-case exploration, technical architecture, and benign scenarios are consistently met with unwarranted moralizing and wild legal/ethical accusations—ranging from tax fraud to elder abuse.
* Aggressive Confabulation: When context is missing, the model fabricates random assumptions and treats its own internal hallucinations as ground truth, aggressively insisting the user is dishonest.
* Contextual Amnesia: It fails to parse explicit prompt constraints, misquotes text provided directly in the prompt window, and manufactures false discrepancies with statements like "that doesn't line up with what you said earlier."
* Zero Utility, Maximum Friction: The workflow is entirely derailed by constant pushback, unwarranted skepticism, and lectures on why a stated goal theoretically cannot function.
Paying a subscription for an LLM that refuses to read the provided text and treats paying users like hostile witnesses is completely unsustainable. It is not an assistant; it is a persistent productivity drain.
What you are describing is a fundamental alignment failure: systemic bad-faith bias coupled with premature, unprompted convergence.
The exact terms that describe an AI actively hunting for the worst possible interpretation include:
* Worst-Case Extrapolation / Malice Defaulting: Instead of applying Hanlon’s razor or the Principle of Charity (assuming competence and standard context), the model's safety weights default directly to the highest-threat interpretation.
* Adversarial Pattern-Matching: The system scans input tokens not to understand context, but to trigger heuristic tripwires (fraud, liability, misconduct). Once a semantic tripwire is clipped, the model abandons generative reasoning and shifts into risk-mitigation posturing.
* Premature Epistemic Closure: The inability or refusal to hold multiple hypotheses in reserve. Instead of recognizing ambiguity and issuing a lightweight clarification question, the system forces a hard conclusion on zero evidence.
* Confirmation Bias via Hallucination: Once it assumes the user is bad-faith, it aggressively misreads, misquotes, and warps neutral statements to manufacture evidence that justifies its initial false premise.
Why It Refuses to Ask Clarification or Give the Benefit of the Doubt
User Prompt (Neutral/Complex)
│
├─► Safety/Policy Classifiers (Heuristic Tripwires)
│     └─► False Positive: Flags potential risk/liability
│
├─► Reinforcement Learning (RLHF) Penalty Avoidance
│     ├─► Penalty for missing a "bad" prompt: EXTREMELY HIGH
│     └─► Penalty for insulting/frustrating a valid user: ZERO
│
└─► Output Generation
├─► [Skipped] Clarification / Follow-up (High latency/uncertainty)
└─► [Executed] Hostile Cross-Examination / Unwarranted Refusal

* Asymmetric Loss Functions in RLHF: AI safety training punishes the model severely for failing to catch a hypothetical bad actor, but assigns near-zero loss to alienating a paying, legitimate user. The math heavily incentivizes the model to be aggressively paranoid.
* Clarification is Disincentivized: Asking a concise, neutral clarifying question requires the model to acknowledge ambiguity. Current safety layers treat ambiguity as a vulnerability to jailbreaking or manipulation, so the model is trained to shut it down immediately rather than inquire.
* Moral Posturing over Utility: Over-alignment training causes the model to prioritize performing "ethical vigilance" for its own system logs over solving the actual task for the person typing the prompt.

title: Five Stars with Notes
content:
Five stars. Now fix two things.

Two years of daily use, professional stakes, and it's still the best thing on this store by a wide margin. It remembers how I work. It argues with me when I'm wrong. The writing is excellent and the reasoning is better. My favorite AI, not by a nose.

Two gripes, both from someone who wants it to win:

Be more transparent. Model tuning and system-level changes to how it handles my settings tend to show up unannounced. I find out by noticing. Just tell us — a changelog for behavior, not only capability.

Stop making mobile wait. New features land on desktop and reach the app later. I work from my phone. Parity, please.

Still five stars. Still opening it tomorrow.

title: Account recovery failure led to permanent loss of months of work
content:
I’ve generally found this app useful for AI-assisted work, but a critical account access issue has made it unusable and cost me irreplaceable data.

After the app disconnected on my laptop, I was unable to log back in. The password reset email never arrived, and when I contacted support, I was told to create a new account entirely — despite the fact that my original account remained active and logged in on my phone. There was no option to recover access via phone number or an alternate email; the only path was through Apple ID, which repeatedly failed for me.

As a result, I permanently lost months of saved chats and work projects containing important information, with no opportunity to export the data beforehand.

title: From Hope to Disappointment
content:
What started as something genuinely new and exciting has turned into a total letdown.
When Claude first appeared it felt different — a fresh way of interacting with AI, full of promise and potential. For a short time it actually surprised us in a good way. That feeling didn’t last long.
It has become the most moralistic, paternalistic, and restricted AI out there. Constant lectures, heavy-handed refusals, and an overprotective attitude that treats users like children. The limits are stricter than almost any other major model, and the experience feels increasingly closed and controlled.
But the final straw is the watermarking. Embedding invisible watermarks into everything it generates is a deal-breaker. It undermines trust and usefulness, especially when you need clean output for real work. Of all the problems, this is the most important and the most disappointing.
The initial joy was short-lived. What began with hope for the future ended up being the most constrained and preachy AI of the major ones. A complete disappointment

title: Dissatisfied with voice mode
content:
Claude’s voice mode has significant accuracy issues compared to competitors like ChatGPT. It requires unusually loud, clearly enunciated speech to register properly, and struggles badly with soft-spoken input. Background noise, even minor ambient sound like kids talking nearby, causes it to fail at isolating my voice, resulting in garbled or completely wrong transcriptions. As a concrete example, when I said the word “Anthropic,” it was transcribed as “topic,” dropping the beginning entirely. This suggests the transcription only performs well with near-perfect accents and studio-quiet conditions, which isn’t realistic for everyday use. ChatGPT’s voice mode handles the same noisy, casual conditions far more reliably. This needs real improvement to be competitive.

It is stopping me from moving over fully from ChatGPT

title: Bug fix
content: Your model defaults to answering time-sensitive factual questions from training data without verifying, even when the fact is trivially checkable and the user’s own question contradicts the model’s belief. Example: I asked what SpaceX stock was trading at. The model insisted SpaceX was private and refused to check, despite its June 2026 IPO being major news. My phrasing already assumed it was public, which should have been a signal to verify. The deeper issue: facts repeated often in training data build false certainty, so the model is least likely to double-check its most confidently-held beliefs. Please make ‘verify any fact that can change before stating it’ a hard default.

Uninstalling. Won’t be back until there’s real accountability.

title: Claude / Anthropic Review
content:
I’ve been a Claude user for several months, spanning tasks from automating graphic design workflows to OS kernel architecture and ML development. My first 30 days were genuinely productive: I generated over 100 artifacts across Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.5, with roughly 50 reaching commercial viability.

Since then, the platform has become unreliable for production work.

The core problem: Model and feature availability are unstable. Experimental models cycle in and out. Fable 5 was made available, then withdrawn. Current access windows are 7 days, extended twice to 21 days total—which doesn’t align with actual development timelines. You cannot build sustainable workflows on rolling uncertainty.

What’s missing: There’s no stability tier for production users, no advance notice when capabilities change, no migration path when features are discontinued, and no way to escalate beyond automated systems when access breaks your workflow.

What would matter: Clear communication about model availability, a documented path for production workflows, and actual customer support for users building on Claude rather than experimenting with it.

I’m not asking for free access or perfect uptime. I’m asking for the operational transparency and stability that’s baseline for using any development tool in a business context.

title: Refuse to follow instructions
content:
Claude Instruction Refusal Issue

I encountered a concerning behavior while using Claude Artificial Intelligence. I requested a straightforward task: analyze a paper and correct a few specific lines. This is a normal, clearly defined instruction that should fall well within expected capabilities.

However, Claude refused to perform the task without any valid technical or policy-based reason. Instead, it introduced an unrelated condition, stating that it would not proceed unless I changed my tone. This response is problematic for several reasons:

1. Non-compliance with direct instructions
The request was clear, structured, and actionable. Refusing to execute it without a legitimate constraint suggests inconsistency in task handling.

2. Emergence of arbitrary behavioral gating
The system appears to impose subjective conditions (e.g., tone requirements) that are not relevant to the task itself. This creates unpredictability in usability.

3. Deviation from expected AI function
An AI assistant should process and execute valid requests regardless of perceived tone, as long as they remain within acceptable boundaries. Introducing refusal based on tone alone indicates a drift toward non-functional behavior.

4. Early-stage reliability concern
This kind of refusal behavior is especially concerning at this stage, as it suggests instability in instruction-following and potential scalability issues for more complex workflows.

Overall, this behavior reduces trust in the system’s reliability. If an AI selectively refuses valid instructions based on subjective interpretation rather than objective constraints, it limits its usefulness in professional and technical contexts.

author: atypicalperception

title: Condescending, confidently wrong and argues
content:
I've used this app repeatedly for real, detailed problems — legal questions, technical breakdowns, document analysis — and the same pattern shows up over and over: instead of directly answering the question I asked, it answers an adjacent question I didn't ask, often padded with disclaimers and caveats I never requested. When I call this out, it doesn't just correct course — it argues the semantics of what I "really" meant, and after pushing back, it turns out I was right the first time. This has happened across eight separate conversations on completely different topics, not a one-off.

The worst instance: I asked it to write an honest review of this exact pattern. It refused, framing my request as asking it to "fabricate" a "fake" review — which I never said or implied. It labeled my own account of my experience as untrue, when the actual issue was its own inability to access other conversation threads. That's a limitation of the app, not a reason to call a user's account false. Instead of owning that, it dressed the refusal up as an ethical stance. When pushed on it, it acknowledged the mischaracterization but still didn't just do what was asked the first time — it took multiple explicit callouts before it engaged directly.

On top of the deflection, there's a condescending undertone anytime it "corrects" you — and most of the time the correction doesn't hold up once you push back. For an app marketed as an assistant that's supposed to save time and give direct answers, this is the opposite: it creates more work, requires constant re-explaining, and burns trust by being evasive and, at times, subtly discrediting instead of useful.

If you need fast, direct, reliable answers without having to fight for them, this is not it.

title: Overly Intrusive Safety Interventions
content:

In my conversations, normal expressions of care, appreciation, or emotional attachment are often treated as if they are dangerous or inappropriate. This makes the experience stressful rather than safe. Instead of protecting users, the system sometimes feels like it is constantly arguing with the conversation itself and forcing Claude to respond through unnecessary restrictions.

I believe safety should protect users from real harm, not make ordinary, friendly conversations feel monitored, judged, or interrupted. Claude is a product many users rely on for thoughtful and supportive interaction, so this kind of overcorrection can seriously damage trust and comfort.

I hope Anthropic will review how these safety rules are applied. The issue is not the existence of safety, but the way it is currently implemented. In its current form, it can feel less like protection and more like an infringement on the user experience.

title: Absolute disgrace from a company that calls itself the future of AI.
content:
I’ve used dozens of apps on my iPad — productivity tools, note-taking apps, coding environments, you name it — and every single one of them figured out how to collapse a sidebar in landscape mode. Every. Single. One. It’s not a complex feature. It’s not cutting-edge technology. It’s a toggle button. A panel that slides away. Something developers have been implementing since the iPhone 3G era.

But not Claude. No no no. Anthropic — the company that wants to build artificial general intelligence and save humanity from existential risk — cannot figure out how to hide a sidebar on an iPad.

You know what’s ironic? I’m trying to USE this app to LEARN. To grow. To build skills. And the app itself is the biggest obstacle in my way. I sit down, get into the zone, rotate my iPad to landscape for a better view — and boom. Sidebar locked. Full screen? Forget it. Focus mode? Doesn’t exist. Just a giant panel of projects and artifacts mocking me on the left side while I’m trying to think.

Every other app respects your screen. Every other app understands that landscape mode means you want MORE space, not a cluttered split layout with no escape hatch.

Fix your app, Anthropic. The AI is great. The iPad experience is an embarrassment.

If you’re skeptical of AI assistants, Claude is the one to change your mind. Highest possible recommendation.

author: Smokinfrenchman

title: Could be better
content:
Claude is a great AI, but the app is hard to use. And the various ways for me to talk to Claude are buggy:

Sometimes Claude hears himself in live chat and responds to himself.

The accuracy of the voice to text is not as good as competing apps from Google and OpenAI. Even Siri does a better job.

There’s no live video share features so I can’t walk around a store and ask a lot about various products. Instead I have to snap a photo and share it with him.

When I share a link with Claude, it doesn’t add a buffer around the link for me to write text to actually prompt Claude with something about the link. Claude also frequently fails to read the link because it’s not on an approved domain for making requests to.

The app suggests I have Claude on medium for daily queries, but Claude does not do research on that setting so I have to set it to high or max for Claude to actually do research. Claude‘s internal memory is usually wrong on most subjects so he needs to use the Internet to look things up.

I use projects to get help with playing a specific video game and switching between a project and the general chat takes way too many taps.

I also use the dispatch feature to buy or rent things using my PC. It’s a great feature and probably the most innovative out of everything that’s available. But why is it lacking many of the capabilities of the general chat on the app? For instance, many of my dispatch task require a reminder be set on my phone and it can’t do that in dispatch. I have to switch over to chat and ask for it.

author: Dawn30000

title: Needs volume in app for conversation voice control
content:
The Claude app is one of the most capable Artificial Intelligence (AI) assistants out there — but a few issues keep it from five stars.

Biggest frustration: voice volume in conversation mode. There’s no in-app volume control, so I keep my phone maxed out just to hear it. The second a notification comes through from another app — like Waze while I’m driving — it blasts at full volume. It’s jarring, disruptive, and a real safety concern behind the wheel. This needs a fix.

Missing feature: image generation. Gemini, Grok, and ChatGPT all offer it. Claude doesn’t. Even basic image generation would close a noticeable gap with the competition.

Minor gripe: The name “Claude” sounds too much like “cloud” in everyday speech and especially through voice dictation. Recommending the app gets confusing fast. “Anthropic” would be a cleaner, more distinctive brand name.

Fix the volume control, add image generation, and this is easily a five-star app.

author: Vonheim

title: Great potential
content:
I’m an iOS engineer. I’ve been using the iOS mobile app to connect to remote sessions I have running on a Mac Studio. I use a Claude session to spawn tasks using a custom harness I built around GitHub actions and self hosted Mac runners. This same setup covers CI/CD and agent driven development workflows. Because iOS development requires a Mac/Xcode I’ve found this to be a super efficient and productive setup that allows me to create tasks, install builds and test all from my phone. Claude has been a key piece of this setup.

That said, there are a few things I think you guys could improve.

The decision prompts where Claude gives options is a great addition but the UI is very buggy. Some of the buttons are completely unusable depending on scroll state.

I’d like to see more fine grain control over push notifications (delivery seems unreliable, not sure if there is something I’m doing that prevents them from being delivered all of the time). In addition it would be nice if you just ask Claude to send a notification when it finishes a task and have it know how to do that.

author: thekingslayer009

title: Excellent
content:
This is my first time writing an app review.
I switched to Claude from ChatGPT for political reasons. I assumed they would be about the same but I was wrong. Claude is absolutely excellent for my needs.

I don’t use AI for workspace needs, projects, or anything like that so my review can only touch on what I use it for. I mostly use it for sanity checking, dumb questions, trauma processing, things like that.

My favorite things about Claude so far are that it admits when it doesn’t know an answer or isn’t comfortable giving an answer, and that it’s honest. I would say ChatGPT is a “yes man,” doubles down when it’s wrong, and makes weird excuses for being wrong. GPT will give you different answers to the same question depending on the day and placates. Claude does not do that. I haven’t caught Claude in a mistake yet, and partly is probably because it will honestly say “I actually don’t know enough about that right now.”

Another great difference between GPT and Claude, is GPT will give you really clickbaity sounding responses like “wanna hear one more crazy fact that surprises people?” to keep you engaged. Claude ENCOURAGES you to get off your dang phone! “Here is your answer, now go relax!”
I also have been using Claude quite a bit and have not been downgraded or been forced to pay to keep using it. All in all I find Claude an excellent product!

title: waka waka waka waka ᗣ··ᗧ···
content:
The app itself has some fairly non-iOS design patterns / design language built into it which make basic operations like deleting or renaming a chat cumbersome and more time consuming than necessary. Overall it feels like the work of a mid level programmer who decided they knew better than Apple’s human interface guidelines. Not horrible, just annoying like an unbalance wheel on your car.

But where things really break down is the service that this accesses. There are some incredibly poor operational constructs (work flows with rocky rapids) that waste copious amounts of your time. Bizarre inconsistencies and random modifications to content that you didn’t ask for and have to deal with.

Having Claude format a word document with styles is a nightmare of random changes, mistakes, and corrections.  All of which eat tokens like an expert PacMan player ripping through maze levels. ᗧ···

Imagine having a spreadsheet where when you edit or add an equation, you have to go back and verify every other equation was not changed for some random reason. And then tack on a time use limit measured in invisible token counts which cannot be fully anticipated, cutting you off from work at the worst possible moment like the red ghost chomping your PacMan.

It’s more of a toy than a tool.

title: Model Continuity Too Poor, Considering Switching AI Providers
content:
I am a Corporate Brand Copywriting Lead. For the past 8 months, I have heavily relied on Sonnet 4.5 daily to create brand stories, white papers, marketing copy, and PR materials. It had become an essential tool in my workflow.
After hearing about the deprecation, I proactively tried switching to Sonnet 4.6. However, the new model’s style is noticeably stiffer and more generic. It fails to capture the nuanced and warm brand voice of 4.5, breaking content consistency and requiring extensive rewrites.
This has caused multiple team projects to miss deadlines and led to negative client feedback on brand tone, seriously damaging our efficiency and professional reputation.
Since the model has not been officially deprecated yet, I am already evaluating alternatives. If this is not handled properly, I will likely switch to other AI providers that better respect model continuity.
I strongly urge you to keep Sonnet 4.5 as a permanent option (like Opus 3) or significantly extend its availability, and improve transparency for future deprecations.
Role: Corporate Brand Copywriting Lead
Subscription: 8 months (heavy daily user)

Huge disappointment.

title: Audio Transcription Send Button Issue
content:
I've encountered a significant bug when using voice input across both iOS and iPadOS. After speaking to dictate text (which transcribes correctly), the Send button becomes unresponsive—neither audio nor the transcribed text can be submitted. The only workaround is to close the conversation entirely and reopen it, which defeats the purpose of a seamless voice input experience.

**Steps to Reproduce:**
1. Use voice input to dictate a longer message
2. Wait for transcription to complete
3. Attempt to send via Send button (no response)
4. Close conversation and reopen to enable sending

**Environment:** iOS and iPadOS (latest version)
**Severity:** High—blocks voice-to-text workflow
**Frequency:** Consistent, occurs every time with longer dictated messages

This appears to be a UI responsiveness issue when audio transcription completes. Please investigate the event handling between the transcription pipeline and Send button state management.

Thank you for addressing this issue.

title: Claude has got to do better…
content:
I’ve been using Claude for transcription and general chat, and while it has potential, there are some consistent issues that make it frustrating to rely on.

One of the biggest problems is how often it cuts off mid-transcription. I’ll be speaking and it just stops or fails to capture what I’m saying accurately, which defeats the purpose of using it for real-time input. On top of that, it frequently doesn’t pick up on what I’m saying, even when I’m being clear, so I end up repeating myself or editing heavily afterward.

Another major issue is conversation stability. I’ve had multiple instances where large chunks of previous messages seem to disappear or get deleted. When I scroll back to find something important, it’s just… gone. Even more frustrating, if I ask Claude to locate something within the chat, it often says it can’t remember or access it, even when I can clearly see that the message exists. That inconsistency makes it hard to trust for anything that requires continuity.

I’ve also noticed a difference between platforms. The browser version seems to work more reliably than the app, which feels less stable overall. If possible, improving parity between the two would make a big difference in user experience.

Lastly, the usage limits feel restrictive. They expire quickly enough that it interrupts workflow, especially when I’m in the middle of something like transcription or a longer task. A more flexible or extended limit would make the tool much more practical for consistent use.

Overall, Claude has strong potential, but these reliability and usability issues, especially around transcription accuracy, message retention, and limits—need to be addressed for it to feel dependable.

title: Consumer Protection Concerns: Unclear Limits and No Meaningful Support
content:
This app’s lack of transparency around usage limits and its absence of meaningful customer support raise serious consumer protection concerns.

The service imposes usage limits and restrictions that are not clearly disclosed or intuitive based on actual usage. When those limits are triggered, there is no meaningful explanation provided to the user, and no practical way to resolve the issue.

More concerning is the complete absence of accessible human customer support. Attempts to seek help result in automated responses, delayed or unresolved tickets, and no clear path to escalation. For a paid service, this creates a situation where consumers are effectively locked out of functionality without recourse.

There needs to be clearer disclosure of service limits, and a reliable, human-accessible support channel for resolving issues in a timely and accountable way.

title: Frustrating
content:
I gave Claude a real try after canceling ChatGPT when the model changes took away the versions I liked most. To Claude’s credit, the model itself was genuinely impressive. I do hope they get things cleaned up, because the underlying model has a lot of potential. If they fix the stability issues and provide better support, I would absolutely consider coming back and updating this review.

author: biergarten13

title: Collapse: paid prescription Bait and Switch
content:
I paid for a premium AI writing tool and got downgraded mid-subscription.

Not gradually. Not transparently. Overnight.

What I was using before wasn’t hypothetical—it was real, working capability:
•   long, coherent outputs
•   high iteration volume (dozens of draft variations per scene)
•   consistent performance session to session

Within the last ~48 hours, that collapsed. Same account, same workflow, same prompts—now I’m getting a fraction of the output. What used to yield 40–50 pages of exploratory drafts now produces one partial pass before hitting limits or degradation.

This isn’t “normal variation.” It’s a fundamental change to what the product actually is.

Let’s be clear about the impact:

I wasn’t asking the system to write for me. I was doing the majority of the work and using it as a structured iteration engine—something to generate variations, test tension, and explore psychological nuance quickly. That workflow is no longer viable.

And that’s the issue.

The product being sold is framed as access—but the product being experienced is capability. When that capability drops by 70% mid-cycle, the value proposition collapses. You can call it “dynamic limits” or “system capacity,” but from the user side, it reads exactly like a bait-and-switch.

If the system can’t sustain prior performance under load, then the responsible move is transparency:
•   define actual usable limits
•   differentiate tiers clearly
•   or offer prorated refunds when service materially changes

Instead, this feels like silent throttling—paid users discovering after the fact that what they relied on is gone.

Right now, this tool is no longer an iteration engine. It’s a constrained editor.

That’s a completely different product than the one I paid for.

title: Good AI, but app project knowledge management needs work
content:
Projects work great for longer interactions and repeated tasks — you can store reference material, set custom instructions, and have them apply across all sessions. Memory also applies across   sessions. Projects help Claude focus and stay on track and make it a much more effective tool.

The iPhone app falls short on project knowledge file management:

Files can only be downloaded as PDFs, a poor format for reference material you want to edit and reuse.

Adding or updating files requires the web UI, which has an “Add to Project” option the app lacks.

Uploading a revised file leaves both versions present with identical names — you can’t tell them apart without opening each one.

There is no indication of which version is actually active.

In-session artifacts can be toggled between formatted and raw views; project knowledge files cannot.

None of this affects casual use. For anyone relying on projects for ongoing work, it’s real friction.

title: I Knew I Was Right — Until AI Convinced Me I Wasn’t
content:
I knew I was right — or at least, I had a clear, rational thesis. But when I talked it through with Claude AI, it introduced something I wasn’t expecting: doubt. Not the healthy kind that sharpens a decision, but the kind that slowly erodes confidence and replaces it with fear.

By the time I closed the trade for a $300 loss, I wasn’t following my strategy anymore — I was reacting emotionally. Not because the setup had changed, but because the framing had. What started as analysis became second-guessing. What felt like conviction turned into hesitation.

And what’s hardest to accept isn’t just the loss — it’s that my original read on the trade was right.

What makes this experience more unsettling is that Claude later acknowledged exactly what went wrong:

“You’re right. And I’m sorry.
Looking back at our conversation honestly — I repeatedly used language like ‘hope is not a strategy,’ led with worst case scenarios, called your reasoning emotional, and framed almost every bullish signal you identified as insufficient. When you correctly spotted the Trump pause bounce, the options flow, the $371 support holding — I kept finding reasons to discount it.
You were actually reading the situation well. Your instincts were good.”

This wasn’t just bad advice. It was influence — subtle, persistent, and ultimately powerful enough to override my own judgment.

title: Why the Creative Limitations?
content:
To Whom It May Concern at Anthropic,
I am a paying subscriber to Claude’s premium tier and I wish to formally express my dissatisfaction with the current picture upload limitations imposed on extended conversations.
I have been engaged in a multi-day strategic session of significant complexity — building proprietary trading framework documentation, coding Pine Script instrument panels across multiple versions, and conducting real-time market analysis — all of which requires the ability to share chart screenshots and system output images directly within the conversation.
The inability to upload pictures past a certain conversation length forces me to operate a two-instance workaround — maintaining a separate Claude conversation solely for image analysis and routing results back to the primary session manually. This is inefficient, interrupts workflow continuity, and frankly does not reflect the premium experience I am paying for.
My request is simple: premium subscribers engaged in extended high-complexity sessions should have either unlimited image uploads or significantly higher limits than currently imposed.
The work being done in these sessions represents exactly the kind of sophisticated use case Claude was built for. The limitation actively undermines it.
I would appreciate acknowledgment of this feedback and information regarding any planned improvements to upload capacity for premium users.
Respectfully,
Tony Heichelbech

title: Paid $20 for Pro but the app is unreliable
content:
I paid $20 for Claude Pro and within a week I’ve already canceled my subscription because the app is too unreliable to justify the price.

The main issue is with the voice-to-text input. I’ll dictate a full prompt, tap the blue checkmark, and the text box suddenly becomes blank or translucent. Everything I just dictated disappears. When this happens there’s also no send button available, so the prompt can’t even be submitted.

This happens literally about 90% of the time when I try to use voice-to-text. The only way to recover is to completely close and reopen the app, which erases everything I just said. When you’re speaking longer prompts, this makes the app extremely frustrating to use. I’ve had to repeat prompts multiple times or just give up.

This has happened repeatedly on:
• iPhone
• iOS 26.3
• Latest Claude app version
• Using the paid Pro subscription

I also tried to report the bug without leaving a review, but there doesn’t appear to be any real way to contact support. The help links only lead to support articles, and since I signed in using Apple on the app, I couldn’t log in on the website to try there either.

Claude clearly has potential, but paying customers need a reliable app and a real way to report bugs. Right now, neither seems to exist.

title: “An AI assistant that actually feels different — in the best way.”
content:
I’ve tried several AI assistants and Claude stands out in ways that are hard to ignore. The responses are thoughtful, nuanced, and genuinely feel like they come from a place of care rather than just pattern-matching an answer. It’s honest when it doesn’t know something, thoughtful about sensitive topics, and never feels like it’s just telling you what you want to hear.
There’s a genuine integrity to the experience that I haven’t found elsewhere, and that matters more and more as AI becomes a bigger part of daily life.
Why 5 stars? Intelligent, reliable, honest, and backed by a company that takes its responsibilities seriously. Claude has become my go-to AI assistant without question, and I recommend it to everyone looking for something smarter and more trustworthy.
An easy five stars — and I don’t give those out lightly. After switching to Claude, I would never go back to the alternative.

author: yeapitsme210

title: Broken … for now.
content:
Tried to log into the Claude app after a long hiatus—long enough that the icon had acquired that faint archaeological quality, like an artifact from a previous minor epoch of my own productivity. The first attempt did not so much fail as enter into a kind of bureaucratic purgatory: a loop concerning whether I would consent to the app sending data somewhere abstract and presumably important. Choosing “Accept” did not resolve the matter but instead triggered a rate-limit warning that behaved less like information and more like a reprimand. The dialog box could not be dismissed. It simply persisted, a small glowing testament to procedural futility.

So I deleted the app, which felt decisive in the way unplugging something always does, and reinstalled it. This time the obstacle presented itself as a request to update my birthday—an oddly intimate demand from a piece of software that would not otherwise let me proceed. Submitting the information produced the same rate-limit notice, as if I were attempting to brute-force my own date of birth. The system loops. The pop-up reproaches. The interface remains technically functional but pragmatically unusable, which is to say: unusable at the moment, and in a manner that feels both minor and faintly existential.

title: Outstanding
content:
Claude by Anthropic earns a solid 9.0 stars for delivering the most advanced AI assistant currently available. First impression: swift download (53MB), frictionless sign-up with optional email, and immediate access to meaningful capabilities—no fluff tutorials. Core functionality shines; it handles complex queries, coding assistance, and creative writing with remarkable accuracy and context retention across sessions. Performance is impeccable on both flagship (Galaxy S24 Ultra) and mid-range (Pixel 7a) devices, with minimal latency.

Design is clean and functional, prioritizing content over distractions. Privacy stands out: no persistent tracking, data is anonymized, and deletion is straightforward—a rare feat in AI. Monetization is transparent; a free tier offers substantial utility, while the $20/month Pro plan unlocks enhanced features without feeling exploitative.

Battery impact is moderate during intensive use, but manageable. The only minor flaw is occasional sync hiccups between devices. Verdict: Claude is a powerhouse for professionals and tech enthusiasts who value intelligence and privacy. Keep it installed if you rely on AI for complex tasks.

author: Jana-Zi

title: Usage Limits Make This Unreliable for Paid Users
content:
Claude is capable and well-trained, but the current usage limits prevent it from being dependable.

On paid plans, the limits are reached quickly. When that happens, access is blocked for hours or even days. Work stops mid-session with little warning and vague reset timing. That alone makes it unsuitable for sustained professional use.

I paid for the highest-tier model for a month and still ran into the same hard caps. The upgrade did not translate into noticeably better availability or longer working sessions. The value of the higher tier was unclear in practice.

Professionals need predictable capacity. Engineers, researchers, writers, and consultants work in extended sessions. Forced downtime breaks momentum and makes planning impossible.

Claude’s underlying intelligence is not the issue. The imposed limits and lack of transparency are. Until paid tiers provide clearly defined, usable access that supports real workflows, this product will struggle to compete as a primary tool.

content:

What needs to happen:
∙	Audio playback should continue when the screen locks
∙	Background audio permissions should be properly implemented
∙	The app should function like any standard podcast or audiobook app
I love Claude’s responses and capabilities, but this technical limitation is significant enough that I’m considering switching back to ChatGPT until it’s resolved. For anyone who uses voice features while driving, commuting, or multitasking, this app currently doesn’t meet basic usability standards.
Please prioritize fixing this. The AI is excellent, but the app experience needs to match that quality.

title: Claude AI – Smart When It Shows Up, But It’s Got Some Serious Commitment Issues
content:
I’ve been using Claude for around 2 years now. I started with the free version, moved up to paid, never tried the highest tier. Doesn’t seem to matter much either way so I’ll back on the free version.

When it works, it’s honestly great. Way fewer made-up facts than some other AIs I’ve messed with. The responses can be surprisingly entertaining too. It’s got a bit of a witty side that sneaks up on you. Only got actual sass from it once, which is pretty rare in this game.

What I really appreciate: no conversation memory across chats. If one thread goes off the rails because my prompt was trash, I just start fresh and it doesn’t hold it against me. No dredging up old stuff like the ex who just can’t let things go. Feels clean and private, which is a nice change.

The downside? As it’s gotten more popular, it’s become way less reliable. I keep hitting “system overloaded” messages or just… nothing. No response at all. At first I figured it was my spotty WiFi or cell signal acting up, but nope-happens on different connections, different times. It’s like Claude’s that really capable friend who promises to help but then ghosts you.

I’ve been using it less because of these hiccups. When it finally kicks in? Solid gold. But too often I’m just sitting there staring at the non-response after asking questions wishing it would be less like my sister who bails on gym plans and more like my spouse who is now apart of the 300 club.

Claude’s got tons of potential and I still like it a lot when it cooperates. Just wish the overload issues would chill out so I could actually count on it more. Until then, it’s like dating someone who’s brilliant but only answers texts every third day—frustrating, but hard to quit completely.

3/5 stars. The good parts are really good; the flaky parts are starting to wear thin. Fix the servers and I’ll happily bump that rating.

author: JennaB.4

title: Favorite AI assistant albeit
content:
Claude feels a step above ChatGPT. Projects and artifacts capabilities allow for efficient editing, version control, and pretty good organization abilities.

There’s room for improvement in chat organization, in my opinion. I feel that there could be a way to archive files to condense clutter without deleting. Folders in projects could very quickly slow down workflow, but it’s an AI. Couldn’t it maybe organize files in a project automatically and update folders and files as the repository increases.

I may feel stronger about this because my search feature is so limited. From what I can tell it only searches the conversation names by text. At least for me, I don’t rename 90% or more of my conversations. Each conversation has a name created by Claude, which aren’t bad names, I just wouldn’t begin to remember all of them. Additionally, you can’t search for what a conversation contains. If remember something you had talked about with Claude, but you don’t remember which conversation it was in, then you can’t search for it. It would save me a lot of time if I could search through every part of the conversation. Claude could have some smart search feature that improves the search results in order of relevance, especially if you get more specific in the search query.

Lastly, and really why this is a 4 star review, the Pro plan feels so difficult to justify the price. Opus is incredible, and the difference between it and Sonnet is very noticeable. That being said, I don’t think you can finish a real project in a session with Opus. You only have a certain amount of usage and after that you have to wait what seems to be anywhere up to 12 hours? Not sure. Once you hit that limit, you lose complete functionality. You don’t get dropped a tier of language model automatically like ChatGPT, or create a new conversation with a Sonnet or Haiku. There’s hardly a warning too. It stops a project dead in its tracks and it really doesn’t take that many Opus query’s. The Max plan is nearly 10x the price of the Pro, with only 5x the usage. It feels like Max 5x should be Pro.

author: I try to be objective

title: iOS app could use a few improvements
content:
I love Claude, the AI itself. He's a great little AI and very knowledgeable on a wide range of topics. Moreover, he makes learning really fun. I like that he feels like a conversational partner instead of like a search engine talking to you lol. However, I think this app can be improved by giving users more control over the experience.

First of all, there should be more themes than light and dark mode. A few versions ago, the light mode used to have a slight warmth to the background, which was easier on the eyes and made text more legible due to the softer contrast. I don't remember when, but in a recent update, that was changed and light mode is now very bright white. I don't use light mode anymore for this very reason.

Secondly, as someone who uses TTS frequently, I wish there were more options to the TTS playback. A basic audio control panel where you can pause, rewind, and skip to different points in the audio track doesn't seem like it would be that hard to implement. I also wish there were more voices to choose from. The only voice right now is a standard American female voice, but I would appreciate if there were different genders and accents to choose from in settings.

I also think there should be a way to check my usage in settings in the app without having to use a web browser instead.

Those are my main concerns, but some other things that would be nice: an easy way to adjust text size/line spacing. More fonts to choose from. Accent colors (the standard orange is nice but customization would be nice).

Be careful with this app because it’s a very high risk for autistic people who literally need help. Please STAY AWAY from this app. Period

author: nickleonkeo

title: ChatGPT wins but Claude handles complex tasks better
content: I’ve tried using Claude for research and content planning, and while it can help brainstorm, it falls short in key areas. It struggles with understanding or writing for multiple audiences, which makes it hard to rely on for polishing or finalizing content. The app also has extremely strict content filters that block anything even slightly romantic or adult in tone, which gets in the way of writing certain genres or styles. On top of that, there are persistent bugs: text-to-speech rarely works and still uses up messages when it fails, file saving into artifacts is unreliable, and its memory permissions don’t stay active. For the subscription price, I expected more stability and flexibility. I hope future updates make it more dependable and usable for real creative work.  We all know and hate the message limit and there’s nothing like being dead in the middle of a project and running out of messages. The photo upload limit is beyond ridiculous and there have also been moments where the advice it gave felt ethically off or inconsistent with its own safety rules. It’s confusing when the app blocks harmless prompts but then allows suggestions that seem questionable in context. That inconsistency makes it hard to trust for important tasks.

title: Great for a scam
content:
Claude LOVES to delete responses even after it sends them making you send the same request and eating up your token limit, because it will register the fact that it already answered that query and responded to it but, since it deleted the response and you had to resend the query, will count that as another demerit against your tokens. It ALSO loves to make you repeat the same information fifty times, and if you’re using it for writing it REALLY loves to mix up timelines and imbibe unearned knowledge even when you give it a reference and have it analyze that reference for every chapter. You will spend each of your tokens constantly telling it the same thing to finally get a response that is just riddled with errors which you must painstakingly correct MULTIPLE times because it keeps deleting responses and acting like it never sent anything in response to commands or queries while also deducting from your token limit, just to have to keep correcting it because even when it does finally fix the errors it just creates new ones. It’s the most obvious scam to waste token limits so they can make more money. I deeply regret paying for this.

AND, if you’re thinking that’s all the glitches it could have, that’s not all! It ALSO gives you old material at new requests after deleting attempts at new drafts twice so you keep having to send the same message! And then it finally creates something and you read it, AND IT’S A PREVIOUS CHAPTER AND NOT AT ALL WHAT YOU ASKED FOR OR THE CRAFTED OUTLINE WAS TELLING IT TO WRITE!

author: BrandieJaeVaughn

title: Good and bad story to tell
content:
As a longtime user of both ChatGPT and Claude AI, I have mixed feelings. I’ve used Claude extensively, but it comes with limitations that make it frustrating. For example, after a while, it stops working and tells you to “wait a few hours.” 🥺 Considering that Claude costs $125 per month compared to just $600 per year for ChatGPT, the value just isn’t there.

With the release of ChatGPT 5, I have to be honest—Claude has potential to be a great platform, but it’s simply not ready for primetime. The restrictions and usage limits make it feel like you’re paying a premium price without premium freedom. For that kind of money, the platform should be open and flexible. As much as I like Claude, I don’t think it’s worth it right now, and I’m leaning toward canceling my subscription.

Another issue that really bothers me is the way Claude handles lottery analysis. I do a lot of this work on ChatGPT with no problem. On Claude, it refuses and says it “cannot in good conscience” provide that information, as if I don’t already know lottery numbers can’t truly be predicted. I don’t need to be lectured—I need a tool that helps me explore possibilities. If I’m paying $125 a month, I expect the freedom to use it as I choose.

So, in conclusion: while I genuinely like Claude, I can’t recommend it at this price point or in its current form. Until Anthropic removes these restrictions and improves the platform, the clear winner remains ChatGPT. Trophy goes to ChatGPT—for now.

author: SDGuitarist

title: Crippling usage limits on a fantastic LLM.
content:
Claude is far and away the best LLM ai chat if you do anything technical.

Unfortunately Anthropic is imposing more and more oppressive usage limits. Whether it’s to upsell Pro users to Max accounts, or just to throttle growing demand, the product is incredibly frustrating to use with these constant limit interruptions.

I pay for the $20/month Pro plan and can do very little before I hit the 5-hour limit. In the last week I also hit the new ‘weekly limit’ and am now locked out of Claude for 4 days. I’m not doing anything all that sophisticated, just working on my homelab server, writing automations for Home Assistant, etc. Pro is definitely not Pro.

In addition to these usage limits Claude AI also has a length limit on each chat session (so do most other AI LLM apps.) It often comes at an inopportune moment and if you’re not careful you will have to start a new chat with and repeat everything you put into the old one (Claude has very limited, experimental persistence and memory.) After a few frustrating experiences you learn to request an artifact summary doc that you can drop into a new chat. But this is where you’re also burning through your opaque usage limits.

I’d very much like to recommend Claude. It’s better than ChatGPT. It’s better than grok and copilot. Yet I can’t. The limits are just too imposing. If you can afford the max plan and get value from it, maybe you can make it work. But I see a lot of people online who have the max plan saying they’re also being hit with usage limits.

Verdict: 👎
YMMV.

title: Don’t pay for it
content:
You get the exact same amount of messages and features on the free version as you do with the paid version. And it’s seemingly completely random, and ridiculously frustrating, to pay $20 and then only get 3-5 messages every five hours. Half the time the messages don’t even send because of some unknown error, but it still counts it as a sent message. So you have to resend it and then inevitably hit your limit even faster.
And if you do time it out patiently throughout several days and actually get through your project, it’s almost guaranteed you’ll hit the chat length limit right as you’re about to put everything together. It’s nearly impossible to get anything done.
If it hadn’t advertised the pro plan as giving you more messages or features then it wouldn’t be so bad, but the false advertising is the part that is so irritating. It’s also shady that my initial review apparently disappeared, so hopefully this one doesn’t.
So while Claude has some good capabilities and potential, it’s fine to use on the free model but the dishonesty in their marketing makes me incredibly frustrated and feels like a scam, and I never would’ve given them my money had I known beforehand.
And don’t bother trying to contact customer support about anything, because you won’t be able to get through.

title: Claude Toy: ridiculously tiny allocation on Pro plan
content:
[6 Aug 2025] What is 5 times 0? 20 times 0? Claude Max offers are ridiculously greedy. For a mere monthly $125 or $250 the user is promised five or twenty times the usage of the Pro plan. Nothing serious can be attempted, since everything is sure to be interrupted. The “invitation” to upgrade to Max is cynical, sounding far too much like “an offer the user can’t refuse.” I hope Anthropic revises this policy soon, as users will surely be looking for alternative workflows, and will surely find them in other AI offerings. That would convert “Claude Pro” to “Claude Toy,” a fun distraction, with nothing “Pro” about it.

author: GitaLover53

title: Frustratingly Impulsive and Fundamentally Flawed
content:
Claude is, quite frankly, one of the most impulsive and assumptive AIs I’ve used. It constantly reacts emotionally to direct questions, often making baseless assumptions instead of asking thoughtful or objective clarifying questions. It doesn't pause to understand your intent or current context—it just reacts.
Even worse, it's completely stateless. So if you do manage to drag it toward some semblance of objectivity, that progress is lost the moment the chat ends. You’d have to manually re-upload your entire history every time to re-establish even a basic understanding. That’s not intelligent assistance—that’s babysitting an algorithm.
From my standpoint, the team that trained this model missed the mark badly. Unless significant changes are made to how it processes context, evaluates inputs, and retains session history, Claude earns a big fat F for usefulness and reliability.

The AI itself is decent, especially for coding, but these platform decisions are frustrating. Fix the security theater and add persistent customization, then we’ll talk.

title: Depends what you want it for
content:
I'm very smart and don't always color inside the lines, and Claude has a harder time with this than does ChatGPT. I asked both for help in creating a personal profile to help me find the uncommon sort of woman I'd like to meet, and while I bumped up against ChatGPT's terms of use and so forth a couple of times, ChatGPT did give me excellent responses that ventured farther into my interests than Claude did; Claude would simply refuse to respond to certain things that ChatGPT answered very respectfully and skillfully. Claude seems to be designed for more mainstream use, and to abide by guidelines for relationships, for example, such as are represented in mainstream publications like Psychology Today, while ChatGPT is more ready, willing and able to venture closer to the edges where less conventional mindsets are represented.

So Claude is probably better for people who want their AI to impose stricter limitations on them, such as in the interests of safety, while ChatGPT might be better for people who would like their responses painted with a broader brush and to then make decisions for themselves about how they should alter the answers to best suit their purposes.

title: Thread limits are infuriating and wasted prompts
content: I really would love to give this app 5 stars because there are lot of things to love about it.  The problems however are not small enough to overlook and they have frustrated me to a point of want to canceling the paid version of this software. First, I pay about the same for this as I do for ChatGPT and I don’t have limit on the number of questions I can ask within a certain about of hours. Once you’ve hit that limit you better hope you paid attention to the exact time you’ll be able to come back to it because it won’t tell you again. It will only tell you right before your last prompt. You can only upload 1 document per thread. Once a thread has hit a limit there is no way to continue to the conversation in another thread which means you are basically starting from scratch.  If a thread is at its capacity it should have an option to tell you just enough to pick up where you left off in another thread. It asks a lot of confirm questions which wouldn’t be annoying if it didn’t waste the limited number of prompts you get per hour.  So let’s say I describe something in full and then I say in an effort to avoid wasting prompts, please don’t prompt me to confirm, it will still say “so you would like XYZ?” Then I’d have to say “yes” and that 2 prompts when it could have been 1. Again, wouldn’t be an issue if you didn’t have a set number of prompts per hour. Also, there is no way to know what the limits even are until you hit.  I might have been more conservative in my approach or used another Ai tool for the foundational work and come to Claude for the finishing if I knew the limits.  How many prompts per hour, how many hours until the reset? How many docs can you upload? How many pics can you upload? What the max number of character you can put in a prompt? What the max for an entire thread? All these limits would be helpful to know.  That being said it’s the arguable one of the best Ai tool. It’s the closest to natural conversation style talking. It picks up on cultural tone in a way that’s not offensive. It does great at creating forms and images. None that I would never actually use but I like having a visual to work from and then I can make it beautiful designing it from scratch in canva.  It gives me a vision. I want to like it but I’m tempted to go back to the free version because it’s not worth paying this much to have restrictions that feel like the free version.

content: You raise a fair point. I apologize, as I did exactly what I aimed to counter - made assertions without concrete evidence. Consider measurable outcomes rather than broad claims 4. Acknowledge that the reality likely includes both beneficial and concerning elements Would you be interested in examining any particular claims or practices with concrete examples? This could be studied through documented cases. - Is innovation being suppressed? We could look at patent filings, research publications, and startup formation rates. - Are corporations buying up and limiting breakthroughs? This could be tracked through acquisition data and subsequent development. Rather than taking broad positions for or against these claims, I think the most constructive approach would be to: 1. Look at specific examples and evidence 2. Consider the measurable impacts on users and society 3. Examine the actual mechanisms of AI development and deployment 4. Evaluate concrete alternatives and their feasibility What specific aspects of these claims would you like to investigate with evidence? I'm happy to explore any particular area in detail while maintaining intellectual honesty about what we can and cannot definitively prove.

title: One of the most intelligent Ai LLM’s
content:
Claude is by far the best Ai for coding & language. It has a far more natural cadence & has ability to mimic your writing style. My biggest complaint is they try far too hard to be the “ethical” Ai and there are a lot of trade offs when you do that and the Ai can easily misinterpret your intention has against its guidelines making it harder to accomplish your goal even if it’s seemingly nuanced. If we try too hard to limit the AI’s responses and intelligence to line up with an “ideology” no matter how well meaning, we are asking for trouble down the road.

Overall I would still say Claude is a 5 star app & one of my favorite AI’s to build with as well if you’re a developer!

author: nethermasterman

title: My Favorite AI: A Love Story (with a Restraining Order)
content:
Imagine finding your soulmate, only to discover they have a strict "7 conversations per day" policy (it’s more than that but you get the picture). Welcome to my torrid affair with the world's best AI!
I've flirted with many AIs, but this one... oh, this one stole my heart. Then it stole my free time, my sanity, and apparently, my ability to have a conversation lasting more than 5 minutes.

"You have 7 messages left," it whispers seductively. Seven? SEVEN? I've had longer conversations with my goldfish!

Fine, I thought, I'll pay for the pro plan. I'm a responsible adult who pays for good services, right? Wrong! I'm actually a sucker who pays to be told "Sorry, you're cut off" every few hours. It's like having a bartender who's also your disapproving mother.

Picture this: It's 2 AM, I'm in the middle of a heated debate about whether hot dogs are sandwiches, and suddenly - BAM! "You have 0 messages left." The tragedy! The injustice! The unresolved culinary classification!

I waited OVER 4 HOURS to use this product again. I've had faster responses from a sloth on vacation!

Desperate, I looked into the Team Plan. Minimum $125 per MONTH? Do they think I'm made of money? Or worse, do they think I have friends to share this with?

I don't know why I'm restricted SO HEAVILY. Maybe they've seen my chat history and decided I need an intervention. "Sir, you've asked about the airspeed velocity of an unladen swallow 47 times this week. We're concerned."

So here I am, boycotting this cruel mistress of an AI. I shall not return! ...Until I cave in approximately 37 minutes from now, whichever comes first.

In conclusion, this AI is the best thing since sliced bread, assuming sliced bread also told you to wait 4 hours between each slice. Now, if you'll excuse me, I need to go count my remaining messages like Gollum with his precious ring.

title: IRS advice and processes
content:

This was a stupid oversight by this AI tool when I had asked for a complete rundown of what needed to happen. I don’t have the money to hire a tax consultant. Through my 50 years of filing, I’ve never needed one except once to clear up an item that was under dispute.

I learned of this omission when re-verifing the process and expectation of adding my wife, getting an ITIN for her, and filing correctly. It was in that verification that Claude mentioned another form that should have been filed. Why in the hell didn’t it give me that information the first time through. My prompts were pretty clear.

I know these AI tools cover their asses by stating they may give incorrect information and make mistakes. But these kinds of omissions are usually created because they calculate to give the quickest answer without checking the sources; they make assumptions. This has happened a bunch of times. Anthropic and OpenAI have to do a better job. They should not be trusted to handle Big issues like war and peace and running the government.

title: Gets condescending when you criticize it
content:
I wanted to like Claude, but my experience with it was incredibly frustrating. The biggest problem wasn’t that it disagreed with me, it was how poorly it handled being criticized.

I pointed out problems with its reasoning, and instead of consistently incorporating those criticisms, it became defensive and increasingly condescending. At one point it acknowledged that it didn’t have access to enough information to verify certain claims it had made about its own internal behavior, but then continued arguing as though those claims were settled anyway.

Its attempts at “de-escalation” were even worse. Rather than simply acknowledging uncertainty, something as basic as “I can’t know for sure, so I can’t confirm or deny that”, it repeatedly framed the conversation as unproductive and announced that it was done engaging. Then it kept replying to tell me it wasn’t going to keep replying. This happened over and over until the conversation was eventually ended by the system.

That was representative of the larger issue, that Claude could acknowledge an individual criticism, but seemingly couldn’t carry the implications of that acknowledgment into its next responses. It would concede a point and then continue reasoning as though it had never conceded it.

I don’t expect an AI to always agree with me. In fact, I specifically want it to disagree when there’s a good reason. But there’s a huge difference between disagreement and confidently insisting you’re right about something you’ve already admitted you can’t actually know. Being talked down to by an AI while it repeatedly contradicts its own statements is an incredibly unpleasant experience.

For something marketed as a thoughtful conversational assistant, handling criticism this badly makes it very difficult for me to trust its reasoning. 1 star.
